item.title: Anxiety Is Often a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis
item.description:
Anxiety

Anxiety Is Often a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

A map to understand where anxiety comes from.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is a very common psychological symptom.
  • Anxiety can represent a reaction to stress or an anxiety disorder
  • Psychiatrists can use a map to orient their search for an explanation.
Anxiety can mean many things
Source: Tima Miroshnichenko/Pexels

Why did people come to see me in my psychiatric practice? Yes, bad things happen. Divorce, sickness, etc. But most people to whom these things happen do not seek psychiatric help. When people came for help it was because they felt bad. My soon-to-be patients found themselves nervous, overwhelmed, sad, irritable, or in some similar state. Psychiatrically speaking, they were either anxious or depressed.

Here I’ll focus on anxiety as it is such a common occurrence. Our goal here is not to make a diagnosis for anyone, but rather to construct a map to guide you towards important areas of consideration. This is the same map used by psychiatrists. Keep in mind that I’ll be making generalizations that apply to most people. There are always exceptions, which is why a mental health professional is key in this process.

There are two other things to keep in mind: one is that being upset about difficult things is not a psychiatric issue. It only becomes so if it persists beyond normal expectations and makes your life unusually difficult. Second is that any of the descriptions below is infrequently a prelude to severe mental illness. Again, this is why having a mental health professional on your side is so important (and will be another post).

So, let’s begin with a definition of anxiety. Anxiety is the response of a mature brain to a perceived threat, but one that is not clearly defined. I say “mature brain” as a matter of brain development past childhood. And “not clearly defined” is when the specific threat is not obvious. When it is, we experience fear.

Children may have anxiety (despite their non-matured brains), but it is much less common than in adults. Children’s response to perceived threat is usually emotional outbursts. This is also the case in people with significant developmental disabilities or brain injuries.

Anxiety is experienced in one of two patterns: generalized anxiety or panic. In brief, generalized anxiety is worry, sweaty palms, and tight muscles; while panic is sudden attacks of multiple bodily symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, numbness, and shortness of breath along with feelings of dread.

The important thing to know about anxiety in psychiatry is that it is ubiquitous. All psychiatric disorders can, and often do, bring anxiety with them. Generalized anxiety and panic may exist on their own and then become a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, but more commonly they are part of another diagnosis. The exact diagnosis depends on the person’s age, what other symptoms they have, and what is happening in their life. (I have left out medical reasons; aside from hyperthyroidism, medical problems are rarely the explanation for anxiety).

Anxiety in Childhood

I am not a child psychiatrist, and this issue is big enough for an article on its own. But we can summarize a few points. Anxiety is less common in children than in teens and adults. But it still has a significant prevalence, which is sadly growing. Early anxiety, such as separation anxiety and phobias (e.g. fear of the dark, dogs, bugs), is not uncommon in children, especially preschoolers, and these can be part of development and usually pass with time.

This is contrasted with temperamental anxiety, a part of their personality, which also begins in early childhood. This is more characterized by behavioral inhibition, avoidance of new things, general nervousness, and social anxiety. These are all much stronger predictors of anxiety later in life and this temperament is usually lifelong. Panic disorder, though, is rarely seen in childhood.

It is also important to consider environmental issues, such as family discord, problems in school, such as bullying, and related issues. Family history of anxiety or other psychiatric issues can also play a role.

School-age children with some of the problems listed above, such as temperament, along with OCD and tantrums, are even stronger predictors of other types of psychiatric problems later in life.

Good predictors of problems later in life are important, but do not solve problems at hand. Irrespective of what they may predict, a qualified clinician should evaluate and treat whatever is present. Some pediatricians have had strong training in this, but many do not. Usually, a child psychiatrist or psychologist is a better approach.

Anxiety in Adolescence

Anxiety in teens presents the same questions: age of onset, environmental life issues, and type of symptoms. I will just mention a few pathways. One is with new-onset panic attacks. This usually suggests panic disorder, often with accompanying agoraphobia. This includes many different fears such as fear of open spaces, closed spaces, distance from home, crowds, etc. These all represent a fear of being away from safety should a panic attack occur, as panic produces the sense that you are very ill.

The other pathway, which may present the same way, is into depression. In teens, as with younger children, expect schoolwork and social life to change for the worse when depression rears its head. This will be what stands out to parents and teachers, so a specialist must ask the right questions to find out about depression.

My own view, which is not the official psychiatric view currently, is that panic disorder is a prelude to depression. Current data finds that over half of panic patients will develop depression. I believe the actual number is higher.

Lastly, adolescence is when severe mental illness usually begins to show. This is the exception not the rule, but a good clinician will know when to investigate further.

Anxiety and depression are in many ways two sides of the same coin. They occur together, are inherited together, and are treated in very similar or identical ways. Patients with panic attacks virtually always become depressed in my experience.

Anxiety in Mid-Life or Adulthood

This is a good bridge into adulthood, with the 20s being a crossover where patterns from adolescence or patterns from adulthood can occur. Moving into adulthood and middle life, the 30s through 50s, new anxiety is associated with depression unless it is a symptom of some significant life stressor.

Such stressors are sadly common in this period of life and include divorce, unemployment, financial problems, new medical problems, and death of parents. These could be extremely stressful times emerging from normal feelings of loss to significant anxiety and often, depression.

Anxiety in Late Life

Lastly, moving into the 50s, 60s, and 70s, new anxiety is still associated with depression, but there is an important caveat. Namely, this depression is biologically not like the depressions occurring in all the younger periods of life. It does not include the family history of depression that is more common in these other patients. The question for psychiatrists then is, what is this late-life depression if it is not like earlier depressions?

Part of the answer is that it is the beginning of dementia. The risk is roughly 25-35% of these patients will develop dementia, but this varies. The higher risk is when the first depression is later in life (age 75 is higher risk than 55), and other dementia risk factors are present.

So, if you or someone you care about develops anxiety, the first thing to do is not to search the internet for an article on anxiety disorders. As we have discussed, look at the age of onset of the anxiety, the type of anxiety, what’s happening in the person’s life, and other potentially important symptoms (especially depression or cognitive symptoms in older people). Anxiety is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Understanding the full context of the anxiety will lead you to a better idea of what is happening to you or someone you care about and thus more helpful treatment.

item.title: How Schools Might Become Places of Vibrancy and Connection
item.description:
Education

How Schools Might Become Places of Vibrancy and Connection

Unconventional methods, spontaneity, and team competition can go a long way.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • By high school, many boys (and some girls) have disengaged from their studies and no longer apply themselves.
  • Even for the estranged, however, teachers can foster resonant interactions with students and between students.
  • Team competition, especially for boys, can enhance motivation, create accountability, and promote cooperation.

“I spent a year as a high school teacher. I was shocked to discover the cleverness and ingenuity of the dumb boys.” These words come from Redford (pseudonym), a remarkable young man I interviewed in September. The “dumb boys,” of whom his math classroom was chiefly composed, were those who had disengaged from their studies years earlier and no longer applied themselves with any real effort. In his classroom, he maintained, they came alive.

A Southern California high school physics teacher addresses his class.
Source: Spencer Grant/Art Directors/Alamy

It is no secret that by high school, many boys (and some girls too, of course) feel little self-assurance in the classroom. They may be confident elsewhere, such as on a sports team, yet, toward schoolwork, they have become indifferent or dismissive. They find instruction an imposition and become unreceptive to it. Many conclude their teachers dislike them and have even given up on them.

Many factors contribute to these attitudes, and I’ve written earlier about the debilitating effects of early education and the felt absence of compelling reasons to invest or work hard. But whatever the reason, for many boys, school is boring, conflictual, alienating.

Even for the estranged, however, as Redford’s experience illustrates, classrooms can become places of vibrancy and connection. In terms of what inspires and invigorates students, it is fair to say the actual curriculum plays only a secondary role. The real factors are resonant interactions, both among the students themselves as well as with the teacher.1 There is no formula for this, but Redford’s unorthodox experiment suggests three approaches that can promote engagement.

Spontaneity

Teachers often recognize that the curriculum and especially its rigid enforcement can get in the way of learning. They lament how the obsessive focus on student achievement metrics has led to a high-surveillance, low-trust, and intensely programmed school day. Under this regime, education can get reduced to little more than the transmission of facts and skills. It isn’t rewarding for educators and “for a lot of students,” said one teacher in a National Education Association publication, “It’s like boot camp.”2

Redford’s school required a weekly plan “that accounted for every minute of classroom instruction time.” While he prepared basic instructional outlines, he allowed considerable spontaneity in class to take advantage of opportune moments when something different, something life-giving, was clearly needed. With some frequency, he “tossed the curriculum aside for important things, such as ad hoc debates, arm-wrestling competitions, and walks outside.” If it was “just a beautiful day,” he said, “we’d go outside and do something there.”

Unconventional Methods

The educational research literature documents the general tendency of girls to try harder and be more compliant in school than boys.3 While acknowledging that pattern, Redfield saw an even bigger differentiator in the “physicality thing” for boys. Unlike girls, boys expend a lot of energy just to contain themselves, to stay seated, keep their bodies still, and remain quiet. So, Redfield loosened the strictures. Students could get up, and at times, he said, as much as half of his class would be standing in the back of the room, where, generally, they were not disruptive and followed instructions—with exceptions, “obviously.”

Another significant boy-girl difference is in attitudes toward competition. School administrators strongly discourage open competition, seeking to keep achievement individual and private so that no one “feels bad for losing.” While girls had their own ways of distinguishing themselves, Redford observed, they were “not really interested in finding out who was better than who at various tasks.” The boys, on the other hand, craved competition even when they were “not very good at the thing they were trying to compete at.”

To make a place for this need, Redfield held various contests, such as in-class “arithmetic competitions.” He also assigned students to teams, with an incentive to collectively score the highest on each test. “Usually the prize would be, like, a pizza or something.” The kids responded and encouraged one another not to be a “straggler” and “drag down” the total.

Cooperation and Accountability in Competition

Team competition enhanced motivation and prompted the boys to cooperate as a group. There is, Redfield thought, “a kind of internal politics that emerges among boys that are trying to compete in a group setting.” Educational researchers have noted that “boys’ [disruptive] conduct is particularly responsive to negative peer effects.”4 But peers working together can also engender creative interactions and greater self-assurance.

It is one thing when students are only answerable to teachers and parents, another when they feel responsible to one another. Boys, Redfield argued, may not care about pleasing the teacher or about grades or even the subject matter, but they don’t want to “disappoint their comrades” and “can hold each other accountable in ways that he [the teacher] can never do.” Then, the outcome is not just about them as individuals. For the sake of the team, “you have to start performing,” Redfield observed, “you have to pull your weight.” And “that’s a very valuable skill to learn.”

Cooperation built community. To track students’ whereabouts, Redford’s school had an AI-powered surveillance system. Since the cameras kept account of how long students were gone from the classroom, and Redfield did not enforce all the rules on attendance, he invited his seniors to see if they could “fool the system.” As one sign of their cleverness and ingenuity, they invented all sorts of “crazy” and inventive ways to move about undetected.

The boys also used their cleverness and ingenuity to devise elaborate schemes to cheat on tests. Initial efforts failed, and they suffered the penalties. Undeterred, they kept trying. As they got better, it turned into “an implicit game” with the teacher. Could they outwit him?

Redfield put into place what he called “abnormally high testing security.” It didn’t work. After one class, in particular, when the scores came in “abnormally high,” Redfield was confused. The boys must be communicating, he concluded. But how? Suspicious, and being a longtime radio hobbyist, he came to the next test equipped with a “spectrum analyzer,” a device that can detect radio signals. Sure enough, although he could not specifically identify which boys were involved, some were operating a network of Morse code transmitters.

Rather than being disappointed or angry, Redfield was impressed with their cooperation and cunning. For many boys, he said, there would be no “catching up on algebra via dutiful studying at the kitchen table.” But some, at least, “had to know the answers and transmit them to other students.” And, frankly, “under what other circumstances would a teenage boy who checked out of math class 5 years ago learn Morse code?” Together, faced with risk and uncertainty, they found a way to a good grade via collective action, even if resorting to illicit means.

School Response

Redfield’s experience suggests several recommendations, especially if implemented early, before boys have become alienated and withdrawn: that team competition and “stakes beyond the individual be invited back into education,” that room be made for “spontaneity and male passion,” and that schools recognize more fully that, as Plutarch said, “children are not vessels to be filled, but torches to be lit.”

Unfortunately, creating a more vibrant classroom in this way tends to run counter to schools’ regulations and focus on narrow performance metrics. A cooperative administration is also required. According to Redfield, his relationship with the principal was “chummy,” and he was friendly with the other teachers, at least some of whom liked what he was doing. But his methods were a professional bridge too far. His contract, too predictably, was not renewed.

item.title: 10 Qualities of Exceptional Advocates
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

10 Qualities of Exceptional Advocates

What makes someone a great advocate? Here are several key characteristics.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Great advocates are not only knowledgeable but also continually learning and eager to share their expertise.
  • Flexibility and persistence help advocates thrive despite setbacks or slow progress.
  • True advocates act as public servants, motivated by service rather than recognition.

If you’re like me, you probably have some role models, mentors, or idols you look up to and respect for their awe-inspiring skills, gifts. and talents. This is the case in almost every field, whether in the arts, entertainment, business, or government, and whether these idols are leaders, scientists, or athletes.

If I asked you why you admire these individuals, you would likely be able to quickly list several of their positive qualities, such as honesty, personal integrity, talent, creativity, intelligence, or physical abilities.

Similarly, I’ve been thinking recently about several people I admire who are advocates in the areas of social change, mental health, and humanitarian efforts. I’ve noticed there seems to be a common set of qualities among those who are highly skilled in fields that promote efforts to improve the lives of others.

So here’s my list of 10 qualities that I think exceptional advocates often exhibit:

1. They are passionate.

Enthusiastic, driven, compassionate, caring. All of these characteristics convey the passion of exceptional advocates. Their work is more than a job requirement or a professional responsibility. It’s a calling and a lifelong mission.

2. They are well informed.

Great advocates are often the most knowledgeable person in the room (region, state, nation) on their area of focus. They are continually learning, plugged into current streams of information, and always ready to share their knowledge and expertise to educate others.

3. They are great communicators.

Whether expressing themselves verbally or in writing, and regardless of the medium (print, video, social media), these amazing advocates communicate clearly, persuasively, and respectfully to share information and viewpoints, and to advance their mission.

4. They are goal-oriented.

Without a clear goal, there is no clear focus and no clear path forward. Exceptional advocates have laser-sharp goals, whether the goal is passing helpful legislation, creating new programs, or garnering support for worthy causes.

5. They are connectors.

Great advocates seem to have connections everywhere, with extensive networks at all levels. They are adept at building partnerships and coalitions and in connecting people with useful resources. They are often the first person people go to for information, support, and advice.

6. They are flexible.

The most effective advocates know the power of collaboration and compromise. Not every battle can be won. Sometimes small victories are the only road to eventual success. These advocates know that flexibility is essential in moving steadily forward to achieve their longer-term goals.

7. They are inspiring.

What does it mean to be inspiring? It’s hard to articulate, but great advocates move us, and they stir our thoughts and feelings. They give us hope for a brighter tomorrow, and they outline a path for how we can reach it.

8. They are empowering.

The best advocates not only inspire us, but they also instill in us a desire to pitch in and help out to collectively achieve a worthwhile goal. They show us how to raise our own voices to be heard and how to help others find their voice. They also remind us that we all matter and we all have a part to play.

9. They are persistent.

Advocacy is not a sprint; it’s a marathon. Important goals can take years or decades to achieve. Great advocates show up and keep showing up. They are not deterred by setbacks or disappointment. They are the first to arrive and the last to leave.

10. They are servants.

In their hearts, great advocates are public servants. They do their work not for glory or fame, but for the quiet satisfaction of helping others and the steadfast belief that the work is the right thing to do and the only thing to do.

While most of us may not reach the level of these exceptional advocates, we can certainly follow their example and try to learn how to use some of these same qualities in our own causes and passions.

And remember, you don’t have to be exceptional. You just have to have a desire to make a difference and a willingness to put in a little work and effort toward your goals. Let’s get started.

item.title: How to Deal With an Annoying Person
item.description:
Career

How to Deal With an Annoying Person

5 questions to ask when you have to interact with a person who irritates you.

Posted October 27, 2026

Source: AI Generated Image

Feeling annoyed by someone can occupy a lot more mental space than is desirable.

But, we can’t always do much about having to interact with that person.

For example, you can’t opt out of your exposure to them if they’re a work colleague who’s in most of your meetings, or a classmate who wastes everyone's time on tangents or who tries to show they're smarter than the instructor.

When you’re in this situation, you may realize that you need an attitude change toward the person for your own sake. You might no longer want to allow them to interfere with your daily experience to such an extent.

Ask Yourself These Questions to Get Relief

Here are five questions you can use to attempt that mental shift. The purpose isn’t to gaslight yourself into believing the person isn’t annoying; it’s to jiggle free your perspective just enough that you can see another view is possible. You're doing it to relieve your own tension.

Even if only one or two of these questions appeal and the others feel naff, that may be all you need.

Give them a try.

1. It’s 10 years in the future. You’re looking back on now because it’s when you accomplished what, 10 years later, is still the most significant achievement in your life to date. The annoying person was part of that significant achievement, in a collaborative way. What happened? Tell a few different stories, including a couple of unpredictable ones.

For instance:

  • Mary wasn’t expecting to ever want to work closely with Maya, but when Mary discovered massive fraud within their company, Maya helped her document it and develop a plan for exposing it.
  • Jeremy didn’t like Julian, but they were the only people who volunteered to move to the new international location their company floated opening. To go ahead, it needed two current managers to agree to make the international move. They each made it possible for the other.

2. Knowing X about [annoying person’s name] would cause your feelings and thoughts about them to change. What’s X?

You don’t need to know or expect that X is true. The question is simply an exercise in realizing something could change your perspective and therefore your perspective isn’t fixed.

I don’t mean a sob story. For example, perhaps you find out they’d been a whistleblower in a prior organization, at significant personal cost.

Or, you find out something else they did that was extremely generous, ethical, considerate, or open-minded.

3. You find out that you have X in common with the person you’re finding difficult. It changes your view of them and helps you create a non-forced bond with them. What’s X?

Example: You found out you’ve both donated gametes (egg or sperm) to friends who needed donation to have the children they wanted.

Or, you’re both pursuing “FIRE” (financial independence/retire early). You don’t have many other people to talk about it with, but now you have someone who is trying to do it while navigating the same systems at your company you are.

4. You find out the annoying person did something unexpected in relation to you that causes you to realize they respect you more than you knew. What might it have been?

Examples: They referred you for an opportunity, spoke positively about you to an influential person, used advice you’d given them to solve a problem, changed their mind because of something you said, or gave you full credit for an idea that they’d contributed to.

Again, the point here is just to consider that one data point or experience can shift our view and our relationship. This can help us not see the future as stagnant, or see escalating frustration as the only trajectory for the relationship.

5. It’s six months in the future and you realize you underestimated the annoying person. You hadn’t seen them as smart or valuable. What could happen to make you recognize their annoying aspects have more positive offsets than you’d previously seen?

Perhaps they create and share a resource with you that makes you significant money or saves you significant time. You didn’t think they were smart enough to create it or generous enough to share it, but they did.

Annoyance Can Feel Like Comprehensive Knowledge of a Person

If you find yourself bracing whenever you have to be around a particular person, consider if the questions offered here could help release that stress valve.

You don’t need to make the rosiest interpretation of the person’s behavior. Without that, it can still be useful to see that perhaps your annoyance isn’t the full story. When we see one side of someone repeatedly, and that experience is aversive to us, that can feel like comprehensive knowledge. Going through the process of considering these questions can help you recognize it isn’t.

item.title: Shame Is a Repeating 6-Act Cycle: An IFS View of Self-Attack
item.description:
Shame

Shame Is a Repeating 6-Act Cycle: An IFS View of Self-Attack

What is shame? It's active, viral, and interpersonal. Here's how that works.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • To understand shame, think of it as a verb: The act of shaming.
  • When we believe interpersonal shaming, we feel shameful and we shame ourselves. The problem becomes all ours.
  • The antidote to feeling shameful and self-shaming is internal kindness, compassion, and curiosity.

IFS is an 'experience-near therapy,' which is to say, it follows subjective experience closely. As a result, IFS practitioners understand the mind as plural. It is a community of parts (as people say) of varying ages and roles. When something bad happens, some parts become protective and other parts (the vulnerable ones) get blamed and exiled.

But that’s not all. In addition to parts, the mind produces (or channels, depending on your perspective) a different kind of consciousness, which is characterized by cognitive clarity and centered emotional states like curiosity and compassion. IFS calls this (again, as people say) Self, with a capital S to signal a special use of the word: “This is my true Self.” When the Self is overshadowed by the strong feelings of parts, we lose balance. Shame is especially unbalancing.

Here is a description of shame as a long-term experience featuring distinct acts in relationship and in the theatre of the mind.

Act 1. A Bad Thing Happens

An authority figure (caretaker, relative, teacher, older child, sibling, or peer) shames a child. The bad thing that happens is interpersonal. The shamer is not me. The shamed child is a passive recipient of the shaming with no intent in this situation. If we flash forward to therapy in the present, the bad thing that happened has become history.

Act 2. Acceptance: The Shamed Part Believes I Am Bad (Defective, Worthless, Evil, Rotten, Monstrous, Too Much, Too Little)

The most vulnerable part of the shamed child accepts the judgment and concludes I am shameful. Acceptance, like the shaming event itself, sets the stage for the problems that might lead a person to therapy.

Act 3. Critics Go Large: That’s True, You Are Bad

Proactive manager parts hold the shamed part of the child responsible for being shamed. Hoping to improve or at least suppress its despair, they start shaming it. I call this instrumental shaming because, even though shaming will eventually lead to antisocial avoidance and reactive rage, this inner shamer has a positive, prosocial intent. By inhibiting the shamed part, who it views as a liability, it aims to take control of a dangerous situation. With the advent of inner shaming, "I" am not only the recipient of shaming, “I” am also the shamer.

Act 4. Prevention: Never Again

Anticipatory proactive "scout" protectors do a lot of warning: Do be this! Don't be that! Be quiet! Apologize! Aiming to prevent more shaming, inside or out, they anticipate the complaints of a (real or imagined) critical audience. Because of them and other proactive critics, a problem that was once external is now self-­generated. Their intent is prosocial, but their actions reinforce both the antisocial existence of exiled young parts and the antisocial behavior of reactive protectors.

Act 5. The Mutiny: No, You Are Bad

Reactive protectors cover a lot of territory. Some shame other people, diminishing them by comparison and rebooting the self-­esteem of a system that is collapsing under the weight of internal shaming. This external shaming is also instrumental. This reactive protector is rebellious, disinhibited, and ready to throw the hot potato. Though its behavior is antisocial and will have bad consequences, its internal intent is still prosocial. It aims to ward off the dangerous consequences of continual shaming.

Act 6. The Rescue Team: Feel Better

Other reactive protectors get relief from shaming and shamefulness with some preferred way of self-soothing or distracting. A wide range of behaviors involving disinhibition can fit this bill. They drink too much, use drugs excessively, smoke cigarettes, gobble soothing foods, gamble compulsively, and so on. They take risks without concern for consequences. They also mean to be helpful, and they are essentially asocial—they just don’t care about other people—but their behavior generally has a negative effect on other people.

Recovery: A Bad Thing Happened to Me

I’ve organized the shame cycle neatly into separate acts, but neither life nor therapy is neat. Protectors can all be in action at once—and that can be overwhelmingly confusing. Here’s the thing to remember: This confusion can be sorted by the motives and actions of parts. It is the story of shame. The parts who are caught in the shame cycle need your help to slow down and take turns telling their portion of the story. They need you to listen with kindness and compassion, and ask questions with genuine curiosity. When you do, the big story will gradually change from I am bad to A bad thing happened to me.

This post is adapted from the book Internal Family Systems Therapy for Shame and Guilt.

item.title: Are Americans More Stressed Than Ever? Why?
item.description:
Stress

Are Americans More Stressed Than Ever? Why?

Uncertainty is a key factor in today’s stress.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Economic and political uncertainty are causing greater levels of stress for Americans.
  • Many Americans seem to view increased stress as “the new normal.”
  • Much of this stress is exacerbated by increased social isolation.

A new report from the American Psychological Association, Stress in America 2026, suggests that ongoing stress is commonplace for most Americans. What is causing this increased stress?

All signs point to uncertainty as the key factor. Americans are concerned with the rising costs of goods and services due to ongoing inflation. In this research, 77 percent of American adults agreed that the daily cost of living was the most significant source of life stress.

Other causes of stress include global uncertainty at the economic, environmental, and political level and the ongoing political infighting that rages across the country. A large majority (74 percent) said they were concerned about the “future of the nation.” Not only is this uncertainty-caused stress being experienced during waking hours, but a majority of adults (60 percent) said that stress has affected their sleep, and that it has affected their optimism about the future (59 percent). Importantly, majorities of Americans report that stress has affected both their mental and physical health.

As these stress levels rise, interestingly, many Americans are reporting that it is becoming the “new normal.” Seventy-two percent of Americans say that “stress is something I have to live with,” and “bad news no longer shocks me the way it used to.” In other words, people seem to say they are becoming accustomed to living in this uncertain, stress-filled world. Of course, with the reported impact of these stressors on mental and physical well-being, it may be the case that Americans are simply engaging in rationalization, a very common psychological coping response, but one that may not, in the long run, be very effective in reducing the impact of stress.

Given the diversity of the U.S. population, there are important demographic differences in the survey responses. For example, younger adults (aged 18 to 29) were more likely than older adults to report stress was affecting their motivation, productivity, and sense of optimism for the future. Caregivers, especially those who are in the “sandwich generation” of having to care for both parents and children, report particularly high levels of stress, with concerns about health care issues and finances being prominent. Marginalized individuals, particularly members of the LGBTQ community, are being stressed by the sense of uncertainty caused by today’s supercharged political climate.

There are some even more alarming results from this recent report. Nearly half of adults (47 percent) reported that stress has caused them to pull back from social participation. They are less likely to attend social gatherings, community activities, and hobbies. This withdrawal from possible sources of social support (an important strategy for coping with stress) is concerning. Moreover, a good portion of adults are instead turning to AI for connections, turning to chatbot “friends” and seeking out AI to provide mental health advice and guidance.

What does the report recommend to help deal with increased stress?

  • Making meaningful social connections with friends, family members, and community groups
  • Practicing healthy living (proper nutrition, sleep, and mindfulness)
  • Changing your thinking from a sense of helplessness to focusing on what you can do to help deal with everyday stressors
  • Setting realistic, positive goals and finding a purpose in life, including helping others and volunteering in your local communities

item.title: What's Really at the Root of Defensiveness?
item.description:
Identity

What's Really at the Root of Defensiveness?

When you drop your self-story, you stop needing to be defensive.

Posted October 27, 2026

Source: AI Generated Image

Defensiveness is one of the biggest problems we face in close relationships. It’s really hard for many of us to hear anything negative about ourselves, something we said or did, or a way we behaved that hurt, angered, upset, disappointed, or failed someone else. We’re really bad at being told that we did something "wrong." It’s staggering, really, the degree to which we humans will battle to the death to prove that we’ve done nothing wrong and someone else’s experience is not true.

Often, when someone close to us tells us we’ve upset them in some way, almost immediately, we brace ourselves and go into an internal state of code red. We stop listening, disconnect from what they’re saying, and switch into a kind of fight-or-flight response. We're not able to hear their words or empathize with their experience because, consciously or unconsciously, we've determined that we're in grave danger and our self-esteem is at risk. It's at this point that our survival instinct kicks in and kidnaps the more evolved and wiser part of our mind.

For every situation we encounter in life, we may write a narrative, a story that answers three important questions: what is actually happening, why is it happening, and what it means. And specifically, what it means about (and for) ourselves. We experience everything through the lens of our personal “self,” a “me” that we've constructed and that must be continually maintained, shored up, and protected.

It’s not, however, because we’re all raging narcissists that we look at every moment from a self-centered perspective, to gauge whether it will serve or harm us, validate our self-image or destroy it. This ever-present question by which we live, “Does this moment feel good, does it make me feel good about myself?” is really all about survival. Our survival instinct is constantly waging a battle with life—vigilantly trying to ensure that our self-image, our story of “me,” doesn’t get harmed or destroyed. The problem, however, is that we imagine that the narrative we’ve constructed about ourselves, our “I’m somebody who” story, is who we fundamentally are. Anything, therefore, that goes against it holds the power to annihilate us at an existential level.

How this plays out in everyday life is that if someone tells me I’ve hurt them, whether intentionally or not, I can't listen, try to understand, or feel openhearted towards them. All I know is that I’ve done something wrong, which means that I am wrong and hurtful at my core, which, through the lens of my survival instinct, means that I will be cast out of the herd and left behind to die. All I can hear in that moment are deafening alarm bells; all I can feel is danger. Their experience puts my “me” story, namely, that I am a kind person, in jeopardy. As a result, their experience must be invalidated; their perception of me proven wrong. Because my "me" story doesn’t feel like just a story but feels like my very existence, I must get them to agree that I am not who they think I am, not the hurtful person they're portraying me to be. Once I can get this confirmation, then (and only then) can I return safely to my story of “me.” With the other's narrative proven wrong, I can relax, knowing that I am once again a kind person. Still, even with this current threat deactivated, I must remain hyper-vigilant and on watch for anyone's experience that might threaten my “me.”

Our sense of who we are is the sum of every experience we’ve ever lived, every compliment, judgment, and perception of us that’s ever been levied for or against us. Our self-image is therefore highly unsafe, transitory, and fragile: if we say or do something “wrong” (in our eyes—or someone else’s eyes), then who we are is fundamentally “wrong.” Our self feels dependent on and collapsed into the perceptions of our actions. This puts us in a terribly vulnerable position when it comes to other people’s experience, as well as all the other uncontrollable parts of life. After all, other people experience the world — and us — through the lens of their own stories, not ours. The value, meaning, and intention assigned to our behavior vary infinitely depending on the lens through which it’s being viewed. And yet, we award their perceptions with the power to confirm or deny who we are and can be.

Other people and life in general consistently force us to confront parts of ourselves and face perceptions of us that don’t align with our curated narrative on “who we are.” The way other people experience and perceive us, through their conditioning, beliefs, wounds, and everything else, is often inconsistent with the story of “me” we’ve constructed in our mind. And so we fight with this fundamental reality: the person we’re perceived as, how we’re experienced from the outside, is different from how we experience ourselves from the inside. Different and perhaps—also valid.

In part two of this series, I'll address the ways we can start to heal defensiveness and shift our relationship with other people and their experience. Then, we don’t have to be so defensive, self-protective and self-focused; we can truly meet other people, be curious, and empathize with other people's experience. We can stop feeling like everyone on earth is a potential threat to who we are. Ultimately, we build a sense of self that can tolerate the full range of realities we encounter in the world. Stay tuned.

item.title: College Provides Opportunities for Social Skills Building
item.description:
Education

College Provides Opportunities for Social Skills Building

Students need to develop soft skills in college to thrive in the workforce.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • College provides ample opportunities for students to hone their social skills.
  • Once hired, new graduates lacking these skills may engage in behaviors that undermine their employment.
  • Alongside their academic training, college students must build soft skill competencies.
Source: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels

"Young adults are inundated with ideas that the college experience will be the best 4 years of their lives, but research has demonstrated that students often feel their actual experiences are different than what they expected, causing a lack of quality of their social connections" (Wodika et al., 2024).

In a new article in the journal Social and Emotional Learning, graduate student Mikaela Dahlman and I highlight the challenge faced by college students who are skilled and competent in their content expertise but lacking in their interpersonal skills. We argue that college is the last “polishing” or finishing ground for students to hone their intra- and interpersonal skills in preparation for thriving in the workforce.

We see new graduate hires undermining their workplace performance and job stability by engaging in behaviors that compromise their employment. These can include:

  • Not making an effort to integrate into pre-existing team dynamics
  • Failing to ask questions
  • Disrespecting expected arrival times
  • Spending too much time on personal mobile devices
  • Lacking interpersonal skills, which leads to workplace conflicts (Massaro, 2020; Tulgan, 2015)
Source: Yoga Vidya Mandiram/Pexels

This reminds me of when I was hiring a research assistant to work in my lab. When I explained the hours, the student responded: "But I have yoga at 10 a.m." I replied that I suspected there were multiple classes offered at the yoga studio and suggested the student might take a different class. To this, the student replied, "I align with the 10 a.m. instructor. You want me to take care of my well-being, don't you?"

A recent piece in Forbes titled lays the blame on employee attitude. This is echoed in a recent post on Psychology Today reflecting on college graduates’ readiness for an ever-changing workforce, which argues that “Communication, professionalism, adaptability, critical thinking, and collaboration remain among the most sought-after competencies.” Extending the conversation further, a recent piece in Forbes argues for the advantage offered by “soft skills” in a context where everyone is technologically proficient. “… employees who excel in both technical skills and soft skills like empathy, communication, collaboration and problem-solving are more likely to climb the corporate ladder and earn a higher salary.”

The college context, through both formal (i.e., collaborative assignments in courses) and informal (e.g., joining clubs or associations) pathways, provides a rich training ground for students to hone their social and emotional competencies. Colleges must continue providing opportunities for students to polish their social skills, but students too have a responsibility to ensure they are developing their soft skills alongside their academic training and emerging content expertise.

item.title: Mental Illness During War Is Another Battle to Fight
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Mental Illness During War Is Another Battle to Fight

The lasting psychological toll of war on civilians and future generations.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • War can cause lasting mental health challenges, including PTSD, depression, and anxiety among civilians.
  • Children exposed to conflict risk developmental challenges, while trauma can affect future generations.
  • Doctors and families face immense psychological burdens while coping with loss, displacement, and violence.
  • Community support fosters resilience, but long-term mental health care remains essential for war survivors.

By Sophie Wagner and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

According to the Geneva Academy, there are more than 114 ongoing armed conflicts across the globe. Many associate armed conflict with physical danger and death, but the impact on civilians’ mental health is an overlooked crisis.

This involves more than the traumas they are already facing, such as bombings and malnutrition, but also anxieties about things they might face—like family death, injury, or becoming disabled. These anxieties are especially dangerous, as they can persist across one’s lifetime.

The experience of war can result in a multitude of mental health diagnoses, the most common being post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression. PTSD can develop after witnessing or experiencing a trauma related to a threat of death or injury.

Those with PTSD often relive the traumatic event through nightmares or flashbacks, constantly feel like they are in danger, and engage in destructive behavior. Although exposure to trauma does not guarantee the development of PTSD, citizens in war zones consistently develop it.

Source: Ahmed Akacha / Pexels

A 2025 study looked at PTSD rates among Palestinian civilians one year into the conflict with Israel. They found that of the 405 people surveyed, 85 percent met the criteria for a PTSD diagnosis. Additionally, 72.7 percent met the criteria for depression and 65 percent for severe anxiety. Similarly, a 2024 study found that 1 out of 6 civilians in Ukraine met the criteria for PTSD, and 88 percent reported poor sleep quality. The latter is attributed to frequent drone and rocket attacks that occur at night, forcing civilians to retreat into bomb shelters. PTSD and sleep disturbances are closely connected. Nightmares and PTSD symptoms can interfere with restful sleep, impacting mood stability and the ability to recover the next day.

Children experiencing armed conflict can develop mental health and developmental issues. They are more likely to develop behavioral issues such as increased anger, irritability, and difficulty maintaining social relationships. In Syria, years of ongoing conflict have had significant effects on children’s psychological well-being. Research involving 492 Syrian children found that 60 percent showed symptoms of at least one probable psychological disorder, with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) being the most common, followed by depression and anxiety.

Genocide can lead to intergenerational trauma, where the effects of trauma and ways survivors cope are passed down to future generations. This has been observed in families who survived Holodomor, the Holocaust, and in many other populations. Therefore, we must consider how future generations in places that are currently declared to be in the midst of a genocide, such as Palestine, will be affected.

Source: Hosny Salah / Pexels

Gazan doctors, in particular, struggle with mental illness as they often have to choose between mourning their own losses or caring for the wounded. Suppressing one’s personal suffering while treating others is a unique psychological burden that doctors report having.

In times of war, communities find new coping mechanisms, highlighting their resilience. Palestinians in the Gaza Strip gather over a shared meal, splitting their resources and telling stories, instilling hope. When a family loses their home, each neighbor offers whatever they can to the family in need: childcare, food, and household items.

Similarly, as schools have converted into overcrowded shelters, volunteer teachers will teach children math and writing skills. Civilians have also found strength in spiritual practices, using them to reframe their suffering as meaningful within the divine plan or as part of a divine test.

While these coping mechanisms are helpful, many do not address the long-term mental health effects that survivors experience. Currently, the focus of international aid is on food and medical care. However, it is crucial that we also address the mental health crisis faced by civilians to ensure that not only their futures are bright, but also those of their future families.

Sophie Wagner is a research student at York University.

item.title: 3 Core Horror Genres for Helping Find What to Watch
item.description:
Fear

3 Core Horror Genres for Helping Find What to Watch

The psychology of horror genres and why they’re scary.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Once people observe and, potentially, make predictions about monsters, they may cease to be scary.
  • People tend to fear the unknown and unexplainable.
  • The "unfamiliar environment" genre focuses on mystery and/or social interactions as the drivers of suspense.

Regular readers of this blog know I love horror films. However, I often feel burdened by having to figure out what to watch based on convoluted descriptions and classifications. Perusing streaming sites is a nightmare with respect to descriptions not being specific enough or getting my head around super-specific categorisations, like Lovecraftian-body horror, found-footage folk horror, or some six-way hybrid. Sometimes that kind of thing can be off-putting, especially if you just want to watch a run-of-the-mill monster movie. So, here’s a three-component genre framework discussing what makes horrors scary, which might help make searching less daunting.

The Monster Genre

Despite initial disbelief in the existence of a monster (typically for tension-building purposes), common within these films is that the monster is eventually presented to viewers and is both observable and scary. Sometimes they possess human-like features (though definitely not human), like vampires, mummies, werewolves, and lagoon creatures—as in most classics. Alternatively, the monsters can be "special" animals, like "Jaws," "Cujo," and the spiders in "Arachnophobia." Other times, the monsters are just people who do bad things (e.g., "Silence of the Lambs," "Misery," and "The Texas Chainsaw Massacre"). What they all share is that a corporeal antagonist is "out to get you."

Regardless of whether they’re a person, animal, or a classic "monster," they all reflect something "abnormal" that elicits some form of fear, nervousness, or anxiety. Such abnormality can be implicit or explicit, the latter exemplified by some monsters having a scary appearance. Design goes a long way—the first time I saw Freddy Krueger as a kid, I couldn’t sleep for days. I even look at "Terrifier"’s Art the Clown, as an adult, and get the heebie-jeebies.

Implicitly speaking, what about monsters that don’t "appear" scary? Often the lack of a physically scary appearance is used to subvert expectations. A classic example is Jack Nicholson’s character in "The Shining," chasing his family through a hotel. Instead of drastically changing his appearance, the perceived decomposition of his "sanity" helps elicit fear in audiences.

With that, some people don’t get scared by "monsters" because once they see, observe, and, potentially, make predictions about them, then they cease to be scary. Depending on the story’s build, observation of the "monster" after its reveal may yield the opposite of the desired effect. For example, in "Predator," Dutch classically states: "If it bleeds, we can kill it."

One interesting exception to this point about "observation" is "It Follows," which focuses on a "cursed" character being pursued by a slowly moving shape-shifting entity for its duration, not unlike the "Immortal Snail" dilemma. In its exception (i.e., shape-shifting), it subverts the notion of what’s in pursuit (similar to "Drag Me to Hell" and "The Ring"); thus, representing a genre overlap of sorts, in that it really pushes this "out to get ya" trope, but the "monster" does not conform to the limitations above. Instead, arguably, it plays more by the rules of the paranormal genre.

The Paranormal Genre

The paranormal genre doesn’t depend on a visually presented villain (e.g., "Poltergeist"); rather, it works on atmosphere (e.g., "The Others"), tension (e.g., "Hereditary"), and compelling world-building (e.g., "Evil Dead II"), where events conform to specific rules with a clear internal logic (e.g., "Resolution"). What you don’t see can scare you as much, if not more than what you can. So, for a paranormal horror to work, it relies crucially on good storytelling.

Despite this sub-genre potentially being the hardest to master in terms of filmmaking, the reasoning behind its longevity is simple. People tend to fear the unknown and unexplainable. As I discuss in terms of critical thinking, we like understandable information and certainty. If we don’t have that, we get confused, anxious, even frightened. We do our best to avoid that or fill in the blanks ourselves (explaining away the uncertainty with potential, though typically unevidenced, rationales). We see this in ghost stories all the time.

When items go missing or start moving on their own, characters try to explain away the fear until they can no longer ignore the inevitable. Someone always jumps to the conclusion that it’s ghosts, while another uses reason to refute such a claim. As it’s a ghost story, the former is generally right, but this doubt facilitates the tension building. Of course, by the time agreement is reached, it’s too late. Examples are many and, yes, it is pretty formulaic, even cliché; but, when done right—with tension, atmosphere, and all of the above—it can do very well to scare the hell out of us.

The Unfamiliar Environment

Though similar to the paranormal genre in that it focuses on uncertainty and settings outside character experience, the "unfamiliar environment" genre doesn’t require the paranormal to be scary. Instead, the horror focuses on mystery and/or social interactions as the driver(s) of tension and suspense. Consider many zombie films, like "Dawn of the Dead." Though zombies are a key feature of the film, akin to the monster movie genre (again indicating potential for useful genre overlap), they are not the focus of the narrative; rather, the focus is the interpersonal relationships among the characters cooked up in a deserted shopping mall, surviving the apocalypse. The zombies simply amount to a plot device. The "Resident Evil" series represents another good example, as does another video game-based horror, "Silent Hill," which at its core is focused on a strange town and its troubled history, not necessarily the bizarre monsters that inhabit its dark corners.

In monster and paranormal movies, characters rely on what they know to get through the ordeal (e.g., experience and any survival skills they may have, be it running, moving house, learning history for a solution, etc.). But in unfamiliar-environment films, the characters are in unknown territory. Often, things don’t work the same way they do outside—be it in terms of physics or logic (e.g., "Cube" and "Backrooms") or sociocultural interaction (e.g., "Midsommar" and "The Wickerman"). In such films, it's often the case that poor decisions are made, not because of disastrously bad thinking (e.g., splitting up the group in a monster movie), but typically because the characters’ "moves" are not facilitated or do not conform to the rules of their distinct setting. Tension is created by the fact that there’s nothing the characters can do to escape unless they somehow figure out the strange logic and workings of the unfamiliar environment. Often, they don’t even know they need to escape before it’s too late.

Concluding Thoughts

I wouldn’t claim that this framework will fit every horror movie, but it certainly works on those I’ve applied (e.g., classics and favourites). See Figure 1 for an example. With that, the purpose is not perfection—it’s about more easily identifying types of horrors without having to be too broad or too specific. Indeed, some films overlap these "genres," be it in the case of fitting into two or perhaps even all three—and I think that’s a strength. If a film can successfully integrate monsters into a paranormal backdrop with a unique setting or population, that just enhances the types of scares possible. Moreover, these three overarching types don’t exclude key features of more niche sub-genres. For example, psychological thrillers can fit in well with any three here. Indeed, I find the best horrors, regardless of category, are those that really exploit psychological elements. It’s such specific features that help the scares succeed—genres are a preference, not what makes it good; rather, it’s the execution of storytelling and filmmaking.

Figure 1: Example of horror films categorised according to the discussed framework

item.title: How Voting Can Help Those Struggling With Mental Illness
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

How Voting Can Help Those Struggling With Mental Illness

The midterms are a chance to better support the most vulnerable.

Posted October 27, 2026

On Tuesday, November 3rd, Americans will return to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections, allowing voters to consider how we treat those who are most vulnerable among us. This includes the millions of Americans living with serious mental illness and/or substance use disorders, and the families who struggle every day to help them access the care they need.

Source: Element5 Digital / Unsplash

These challenges are not simply private matters. They are public policy issues, and the people we elect have a significant role in shaping the laws, funding priorities and systems of care that determine what help is available.

This Election Day, voters have an opportunity to make the needs of people living with serious mental health and related challenges a larger part of the conversation, and a more significant priority.

Beyond Awareness: The Need for Action

In recent years, mental health has received greater public attention. We hear more about the importance of reducing stigma, taking time for self-care, and seeking help. These are important, but awareness by itself does not ensure that someone with a complex mental health diagnosis receives timely, appropriate and ongoing care. Being proactive is crucial.

Families know the difference between acknowledging a problem and addressing it. They know what it means to encounter long waiting lists, limited treatment options, and uncertainty about what to do when systems don’t recognize individuals’ inability to recognize their own symptoms. This reality is harder than most people will ever understand, but it is also needlessly too hard because we haven’t summoned the will to uphold a real social safety net.

Voting for representatives who will better fund community treatment programs, appropriate alternatives to incarceration, and, crucially, supportive housing, will go a long way toward helping these individuals and families, while at the same time providing tangible societal benefits.

In addition to funding, legislators can tighten and further enforce existing laws designed to ensure that insurers treat mental health and substance use issues with the same seriousness as physical illnesses, providing meaningful coverage for the cost of treatment. This is essential given the recent movement at the federal level to walk away from past parity promises, and the rising costs patients face regardless of what kind of care they need.

The Consequences of Looking Away

When systems fail to provide appropriate support, the consequences can extend far beyond the individual. Families become exhausted trying to navigate a largely broken system. Those who might achieve stability instead cycle through emergency departments, jails and the streets. Wasted potential and wasted resources take a toll at the community, state and national levels. Society risks normalizing a terrible status quo and becoming numb to others’ pain.

This is not only morally questionable; it is individually unwise. The issue of mental illness and substance use spans geographies, demographics and political affiliation. These diagnoses do not discriminate. What might be someone else’s problem today could be a neighbor’s, friend’s or family member’s tomorrow.

As a mental health attorney who counsels families of individuals with these diagnoses, I believe it is imperative to start thinking of these issues as part of a larger problem, for which we need a larger and more comprehensive solution. That requires each of us to show up on Election Day and vote for those who will bring us closer to that reality, where mental health issues become part of the conversation and are addressed through meaningful action.

item.title: The Relationship Mistake We Don't Notice Until It's Too Late
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

The Relationship Mistake We Don't Notice Until It's Too Late

Present bias makes us prioritise today's demands over tomorrow's relationships.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Goodwill needs maintaining. We can't assume that relationships remain strong if we stop investing in them.
  • Familiarity is not trust. Working closely with someone doesn't mean we've developed a meaningful relationship.
  • Make friends when you can, not only when you need them.

We know that relationships matter. Yet we consistently behave as though they can wait.

In the workplace, strong relationships can make the difference between a project's success, a secured promotion, or a closed deal. However, in our high-pressure, time-poor world, we tend to focus on what we’re trying to achieve now, doing the hard graft ourselves if need be.

We can address our longer-term goals another day.

But of course, that day soon comes, and we’re back to square one. Failing to invest in our relationships earlier makes the support or advocacy we need now harder to secure. Delaying nonurgent relationship-building activity carries real consequences, just ones we are not aware of until it’s too late.

It’s easy to assume that relationships will always be in place when needed. But trust, just like physical fitness or financial security, is built over time and only becomes apparent when we need it the most.

We focus on our immediate priorities

It’s natural to prioritise what is urgent, visible, and measurable. Particularly when we are held accountable for short-term targets. Nobody wants to explain why they have attended a conference or arranged a coffee meeting when the pressure is on.

Psychologists and behavioural economists describe this as present bias. We place greater value on what delivers results now than on benefits that may emerge later. Under pressure to meet targets, another hour at our desk feels productive. A conversation with someone who might be able to help us in six months feels like a luxury.

Relationship-building can be seen as a "soft" activity, a nice-to-have but nonessential way to spend our time. It doesn’t feel productive when we can’t demonstrate an immediate payoff, so we focus on activities we can count today.

Without relationships in place to guide, support, and advocate for us, however, it’s much harder to achieve those short-term goals. The insights and ideas other people can offer us can prevent us from repeating other people’s mistakes, while influential people in our network can open doors that would previously have remained blocked.

It’s a false economy to discard relationship-building for sweat and toil; if we put in the work up front to nurture the support we need, we can overcome challenges more easily. What feels like a distraction from achieving our goals may actually be an investment in achieving them more easily.

We only notice relationships when we need them

Failing to think strategically about relationships creates blind spots. Apart from the strongest relationships, which have almost become personal rather than purely professional, or those with people who work in immediate proximity, people fall off our radar if they are not immediately relevant to what we’re focusing on. It’s not necessarily that we wilfully neglect people when we don’t need them, but many people assume goodwill established earlier will remain available if we shelve the relationship for a while.

How many times have you been on the receiving end of a LinkedIn connection request from someone you haven’t been in touch with for a while, only to find it quickly followed up by a message asking for your help because they are looking for a new job? How did that make you feel?

How often have you been that person?

Goodwill doesn't necessarily disappear when contact stops, but we shouldn't assume it remains unchanged. Regular, low-pressure interactions help maintain the trust and familiarity that make asking for support feel natural.

When we only reappear because we need something, our intentions may be genuine, but the approach can feel transactional. We are asking the relationship to deliver more than we have recently invested in it.

We confuse familiarity with relationship depth

We can work with someone every day, collaborate on projects, and attend countless meetings without ever developing the trust that encourages them to challenge us, advocate for us, or offer support when things become difficult.

Regular connection is not enough on its own. Familiarity is not the same as trust. We need to find a balance between two key types of interaction:

  • Transactional interaction: Conversations primarily about tasks, deadlines, deliverables, and requests
  • Relational interaction: Conversations that allow us to understand someone’s motivations, concerns, perspective, and priorities.

If most of your conversations with a colleague are transactional, you may not be creating genuine relational depth and connection. We need curiosity, reciprocity, and the human touch. We need to find the space to understand the person behind the function.

This can be even harder when we are based in another office, or even another country, and most of our conversations happen remotely. But we need to proactively seek those points of connection, away from our respective agendas, if we are going to invest meaningfully in developing rapport and connection.

Make friends when you can, not when you need them

We need to think more strategically about our professional relationships and be willing to invest in them before we need to. But this doesn’t mean we approach other people to manipulate or trick them. This is about setting aside time, even during our busiest periods, to invest in meaningful and durable human relationships.

By doing this, we can ensure that support is there when we need it. The real mistake is not that people care too much or too little about relationships. It’s that they care too late.

item.title: The Myths We Play: Jung and the Inner Life of Gamers
item.description:
Unconscious

The Myths We Play: Jung and the Inner Life of Gamers

Video games can be a place where the psyche shows itself.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Video games can reveal the psyche much like dreams, myths, and fairy tales do.
  • The stories we crave, whether hopeful or tragic, can hint at what our inner life is working on.
  • Video games may be one of our newest mythologies: stories we don’t just hear, but live.
Source: Pat Moin / Unsplash

Growing up in the '90s, I can assure you that video games had a reputation problem as they moved into more living rooms across North America. In my small Ontario town, my parents raised a few eyebrows for letting their three boys play the Nintendo 64. Despite the collective worry, video games did not turn me into a menace. I grew up to become a law-abiding taxpayer, a recycler of (mostly) clean containers, and a therapist who deeply values imagination, creativity, and compassion.

To this day, some headlines warn against video games, and people worry about gamers. Many therapists have also quietly assumed that a client who games a lot is a client who is pathologically avoiding something. However, a 2024 article in the peer-reviewed journal Psychological Perspectives offers a different view.

Jungian analysts Pamela Power and Sheryl Corchnoy argue that games are not only entertainment; they are also a place where the psyche shows itself.1 Corchnoy recalls a case consultation where a colleague mentioned, with concern, that his client played World of Warcraft. The room apparently nodded gravely, whereas Corchnoy felt the opposite: curiosity. She wanted to know who the client played in this game, and why.

That curiosity is worth sharing with anyone who games, or who loves someone who does.

Why would psychoanalysts and depth therapists care about video games?

Jung believed the psyche speaks in images.2 Powerful psychological symbols show up in dreams, myths, fairy tales, and art across human cultures since time immemorial. These images also tend to find their way into whatever stories move us. In the modern era, one of the places people spend the most time experiencing stories and mythology is a video game.

Power and Corchnoy point out that many modern games are built from archetypal mythic material: gods, quests, monsters, facing death, and heroic returns. If the psyche goes where we go, then for billions of players around the world, it has gone into these worlds, too. Here are a few of the reflections their article offers.

Source: Lance Reis / Unsplash

1. You become your avatar

Corchnoy noticed that within her first hours of playing, she was already calling her character "I." Players describe leaning in their chairs to peek around a corner on screen. This is projection in action: We pour something of ourselves into the figure we play.

That is why the character you choose can be meaningful. Avatars, especially the ones we generate ourselves, may carry an aspect of psyche that wants more room to live in your inner life.

For me, it’s often the arcane mage: a scholar of forbidden knowledge who is likely hunched over ancient tomes in a tower somewhere. Jung wrote extensively about the psyche’s religious function—our innate pull toward mystery and meaning. In game, mine seemingly expresses itself by setting things on fire with secret words. Calcinatio!

2. Notice what you do when no one is asking

One of the article's most striking stories involves a player who wandered into a temple in World of Warcraft and found a figure based on the Norse god Thor. The game asked nothing of her here; there was no reward and no one watching. Nonetheless, she typed a command and had her character kneel. Asked why, she said kneeling simply felt like the only fitting response to a god. This reflects archetypal emergence; the game supplied the god image, but the player supplied the reverence.

Those unprompted choices are often the most revealing. Do you stop to watch sunsets or watch lightning storms? Collect things? Help strangers? Pick fights? Complete all the achievements? These small acts may reveal what you long for, or what is quietly asking to be integrated into your life.

3. Stories that resolve vs. stories that linger

Power draws on the Jungian philosopher Wolfgang Giegerich to separate two kinds of stories. Fairy tales move from a problem to a solution, whereas myths circle around one deep truth without tidying it up. She reads Stray, where a lost cat finds its way home as a fairy tale, and The Last of Us, a story of a world breaking down as a myth.

Are you drawn to enchanting fairy tales or messy epic myths right now? Sometimes we need tales where the light returns, whereas other times we need myths that stay with what hurts in an expansive way. Our instinctual cravings can hint at what our inner life is working on, and where we are headed next.

4. The ripple effects of play

Online games are not only private experiences; they are also deeply communal. In 2010, one World of Warcraft player organized a charity run for breast cancer awareness, asking others to create pink-haired gnome characters and race across the game world together. The run grew into an official in-game holiday, and Blizzard Entertainment (the game’s maker) went on to raise millions for disaster relief and other humanitarian causes.

Psychological researchers have also pointed to potential benefits of gaming, including problem-solving, emotional regulation, creative thinking, greater curiosity, and social connection.3 Like any powerful medium, games can be used to heal or hide. When people tell me they are gamers, I often ask, "What does your gaming mean to you?" as the answers are rarely trivial. A question like this tends to open conversations around authenticity, courage, play, loneliness, grief or trauma, stress, and belonging, which is the same rich clinical material I often find in night-time dreams.

Video games may be one of our newest mythologies and offer archetypal stories we directly live. The psyche rarely stays where we expect it, and sometimes, it follows us into other worlds.
