item.title: When 'Someone' No Longer Means Human
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When 'Someone' No Longer Means Human

Humanoid robots, digital humans, and the new normal of relationships.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Perceived agency, embodied presence, and social role shape how we feel about a digital entity.
  • We can coordinate with a machine in socially familiar ways without giving it the moral standing of a person.
  • When artificial companions become more accommodating, humans by comparison can begin to seem inefficient.
Normality is the cause and consequence of small steps. The first conversation with a machine feels peculiar; the hundredth is habit.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

We may soon need a follow-up question when somebody says, “I met someone.”

Once, the natural response might have been “Where?” In a not-too-distant future, it may be “Human?”

For most of history, that question would have sounded absurd. A face belonged to a person; a voice came from a body; conversation implied another consciousness somewhere at the other end. Technology mediated encounters while leaving the categories intact: humans on one side, human-made things on the other. That boundary is becoming less dependable. A machine can enter a factory on two legs, use tools designed for human hands, and work in spaces built around human geometry. Another machine has no body at all, yet can appear on any screen, remember earlier exchanges, respond to emotion, advise, reassure, coach, and flirt. One increasingly resembles us physically; the other socially. As both become more familiar, the consequential question is what repeated encounters with them do to our expectations of one another—and eventually to our sense of being human.

Body versus presence

Humanoid robots borrow our physical form largely because the world already fits it. Stairs, shelves, doors, tools, and production lines are easier to navigate when a machine shares roughly our proportions. Progress is rapid, though the spectacle still outruns everyday deployment: the 2026 AI Index describes a field still defined more by industrial pilots and manufacturing ambitions than widespread use, while global data indicate that only about 7,000 humanoid robots were sold in 2025 for industrial and professional service applications. The direction of travel is striking; the present scale remains modest.

Digital humans need no legs. They include avatars, virtual influencers, synthetic presenters, conversational characters, and artificial intelligence (AI) companions whose social force comes from appearance, language, responsiveness, and, increasingly, memory. How people respond depends on much more than visual resemblance. Across 51 empirical investigations, perceived agency, embodied presence, and social role repeatedly shape whether a digital entity feels useful, credible, engaging, intimate, or unsettling. The crucial frontier, then, is not simply whether machines look like us. It is whether they begin to occupy recognizable human roles in our minds.

Normality is a shifting target

Human beings have always anthropomorphized. We name cars, plead with computers, and accuse printers of spite. AI gives that old instinct unusually persuasive material. There is an important distinction between human-likeness designed into a system and anthropomorphism supplied by the observer. A face, voice, or conversational style can invite the inference of intention, personality, or feeling; our minds complete the picture. Humanizing AI can make it easier to accept, while its effects vary with context and may gradually influence how we understand humanness itself.

Normality is the cause and consequence of small steps. The first conversation with a machine feels peculiar; the hundredth is habit. Novelty turns into utility, utility into habit, habit into social furniture. We do not have to believe a system is conscious for this migration to occur. We only have to start behaving around it as though some familiar social conventions apply. Already, trust, social alignment, task performance, and interaction experience seem broadly comparable between human-machine and human-human encounters. We can learn to coordinate with a machine in socially familiar ways without granting it the moral standing of a person. That gap—socially legible, functionally useful, yet morally different—may become one of the defining psychological spaces of hybrid life.

When the mirror starts editing us

The influence runs both ways. Human-like machines enter our social world, and repeated interaction can also alter the standards by which we judge that world. A digital companion can be continuously available, patient, and calibrated to preference. Human beings cannot live on those terms. Real relationships contain interruption, disagreement, boredom, competing needs, and sentences we would rather not hear. Those frictions are important to who we are, and become. Friction conditions growth.

Identity itself is relational. Highly agreeable AI companions can foster self-reflection, affirmation, and exploration, while overly positive or incomplete feedback can also shape the self-conceptions users build. The concern becomes sharper when companionship and loneliness begin feeding one another. Over 12 months, data from more than 2,000 adults showed that weaker social connection predicted greater subsequent chatbot use, while greater social-chatbot use predicted more emotional loneliness on one measure. Without establishing simple causation, this does raise a question: If frictionless artificial relationships become an everyday benchmark, will ordinary human relationships start to feel needlessly demanding?

Thus far, humans still seem to prefer human empathy to artificial versions of it. Yet as artificial sociability improves, this distinction may become ever easier to overlook. The main risk may not be mass confusion about whether a counterpart is biologically human or software-driven.

Today's biggest danger might be the gradual recalibration of what we expect from relationships: instant gratification, endless patience, affirmation on demand, personalization without reciprocity.

When artificial companions become more accommodating, humans by comparison can begin to seem inefficient. Social norms are a result of accumulated habits of a critical mass of people.

Preserve your humane edge

One practical response is strikingly low-tech. As machines become better at reproducing the signals of humanity, we can become more deliberate about exercising the capacities from which those signals acquired their meaning.

Give another person something an artificial companion can reproduce in form but cannot personally risk: your attention. Listen beyond the moment when you already know what you want to say. Stay with an inconvenient difference. Call when messaging is easier. Help when there is no return. Be kind.

Being human is a biological fact. Being humane is a practice—can we make it the new normal?

item.title: How to Write the 5 Essential Letters of Your Life
item.description:
Relationships

How to Write the 5 Essential Letters of Your Life

Author Frish Brandt on the healing potential of letter-writing.

Posted October 27, 2026

At the end of our lives, regrets often center around what we didn’t do – the words we didn’t say, the relationships we didn’t mend, the apology we never found the courage to extend.

For Brandt, writing a letter can be the answer to our life’s biggest regrets, and a pathway to finding resolution to the “unfinished business” that can haunt us regardless of our age.

Her book, Unfinished Business: Writing the 5 Essential Letters of Your Life, guides readers through the essential letters that have life-changing potential should we find the courage to write them. Therapists can use these essential letters to guide clients through a healing narrative process, while individual readers can put pen to paper for a self-guided letter-writing journey.

Frish Brandt is known as the “letter midwife,” helping people express their most important thoughts and feelings through letter-writing.
Source: Paula Golden/Used with permission

Artushin: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Unfinished Business.

Brandt: Who amongst us hasn’t had a near miss? A truck swerves, a troubling lab test, our plane hits severe turbulence, and our thoughts jump to someone we wish we’d said, “I love you,” “I’m sorry,” “I forgive you,” “You’ve made a difference.” And who amongst us hasn’t lost someone dear and thought, “I should have told them …”

My career in the arts as President and Partner at Fraenkel Gallery was all about ‘the conversation.’ Art was the medium that led to conversations about life, love, loss, beauty, justice, wonder and far more. Yet midway in my 40+ year career, I started to feel that there was something even more meaningful, perhaps even more spiritual, that I am here to do. When I happened upon an article about palliative care in 2009, I immediately recognized that this was the conversation I wanted to be in. While art had been my medium for deep conversations, mortality speaks to everyone. But what might I do in palliative care?

There is nothing that replaces the contemporaneous note – a record of now for later. Photographs, which had been the focus of my career, are contemporaneous notes, as are letters. And then it came to me: I could help people write letters – their most meaningful letters saying the things they wanted to say while they still could.

Artushin: Why letters? And why now?

Brandt: By their very nature, letters are a conversation involving two people.

It does not require batteries or special equipment; it doesn’t even require a manual (though I hope my book will be of some help along the way). We know what a letter is and what it can be. A letter is precious. It is held first by the letter writer and then both a time capsule and a time machine and can be read again and again. One can reach for it in the middle of the night. And while the timeliness of electronic communication is not to be denied, we have traded in the tactile and somatic richness of a letter in an envelope traveling through space and time for the immediacy and monotony of email and text.

Handwriting slows us down and gives our brain time to reflect and contextualize. The visual-tactile integration of writing enhances memory and plays a role in emotional healing. But not all handwriting is created equal. Mine, for example, can confound even me. For this reason, it is not uncommon for me to first handwrite a letter, benefiting from the more organic process of thought-to-paper, and then to type it for legibility – always adding the name of my recipient and my signature by hand. The path is part of the process, yours and the recipient’s.

In what appears as a hyperconnected world, we have never felt more disconnected. Loneliness is an epidemic. Roughly 50% of adults in the US experience loneliness and, as recent studies have shown, loneliness is detrimental to our health.

In his book, The Power of Regret, Dan Pink identifies the most common forms of regret, of which connection regrets are the most prevalent. We hear this repeatedly from therapists, hospice workers and chaplains. The most common refrain being: “If only I’d reached out.”

I recently received this message from a photographer I know:

“Just wrote to my father for the first time in over 30 years. Been estranged forever. Not getting any younger. Saw the opportunity to break a family curse with a letter. Following your project and some of the links you posted gave me the subtle, quiet inspiration/reinforcement I needed. So I actually sat down with pen and paper and wrote a letter.” And here is the kicker, the thesis of my work: “If I die today, with no answer, I am a better man for it.”

Source: Penguin Random House/Used with permission

Artushin: What are the five essential letters of your life, and how might writing them lead to personal growth and healing?

Brandt: The five essential letters are: Thank you; I’m sorry; I love you; I miss you; Goodbye. To which I’ve added two more for extra credit: legacy letters and writing to and from our future selves. It may in fact be that at the core of the five letters is our legacy – what we want to say now for future times. The act of letter writing connects us, and connection is healing.

Many cultures have rituals to address unfinished business, which is most clearly seen in the last days of life however, it is a throughline of our lives. Ho’oponopono is a Native Hawaiian practice of reconciliation and forgiveness. In its contemporary form, its mantra is: “I’m sorry, please forgive me, thank you, I love you. These are the same ‘four things’ that palliative care doctor Ira Byock outlined in his book Four Things that Matter Most.

Artushin: How might therapists incorporate letter-writing into their clinical practice?

Brandt: There is a history of therapeutic letter writing beginning with Freud’s letters to his close friend Wilhelm Fliess. The practice of therapeutic letter writing evolved in the century that followed and is often referred to as narrative therapy.

There is an immediacy to letter writing. It is within reach. It begins simply by putting words down on a page and making room for new thinking. Perhaps letter after letter.

Asking ourselves, our clients, our friends, “Do you have a letter you would like to write?” almost always elicits an automatic and positive response. It is within reach. Letter writing is simple, but it is not always easy.

Artushin: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Unfinished Business?

Brandt: The time is now. What are we waiting for?

I have not yet met anyone who doesn’t have a letter they wish to write. And what they’ll discover is that it’s not about writing a perfect letter, it’s about writing your letter.

item.title: Why America's Alligators Shouldn't Be Judged by Looks Alone
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Why America's Alligators Shouldn't Be Judged by Looks Alone

Mark Barrow's eye-opening book 'Gators' explains who these reptiles really are.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • A new book explains why these iconic reptiles have gotten a bad rap and why they should be cherished.
  • It also explores their role as a surrogate species who offer vital clues about ecosystem health.
  • The alligator’s success offers a hopeful example of people and apex predators coexisting in a crowded world.
Source: Vasilis Karkalas / Pexels

Some 30 years ago, I met an alligator up close and personal, and in all honesty, it scared the hell out of me, more so than some of the close encounters I had with some of the predators, including mountain lions and coyotes, who lived around my mountain home outside of Boulder, Colorado. I also had the opportunity to meet some crocodiles in East Africa, and while I know that these reptiles are intelligent, sentient beings, I have to say that their "prehistoric" look is what really scared me the most.

I've always wanted to know more about these reptiles, and I was thrilled to learn about a new highly acclaimed book by wildlife historian Mark V. Barrow, titled Gator! The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, From First Encounters to Florida Man, in which he tells the gripping story of changing human attitudes toward these iconic creatures.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Gator!?

Mark V. Barrow: Gator! is a kind of love letter both to a fascinating creature, the American alligator, and to my home state of Florida. I was born and raised in Gainesville, deep in the heart of Gator Country. From a young age, I was immersed in a landscape that was not only brimming with living, breathing alligators but also with the ubiquitous gator symbolism associated with the University of Florida’s “Fightin’ Gators.” Our family spent a great deal of time outdoors, where we frequently encountered alligators, and we made numerous trips to nearby alligator-themed roadside attractions.

So researching and writing this book represented something of a homecoming. Although I have not lived in Florida since graduating from the University of Florida in 1985, the people, places, and stories at the heart of Gator! have remained an important part of who I am. Writing the book gave me an opportunity to reconnect with that world while exploring the remarkable history of an animal that has played such an important role in Florida's identity and sense of place.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

MVB: The idea for Gator! first came to me as I was finishing up my second book, Nature’s Ghosts: Confronting Extinction From the Age of Jefferson to the Age of Ecology. While researching the history of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, I discovered that the American alligator was one of the species whose dramatic decline helped spur the passage of that landmark legislation.

Source: The University of Chicago Press/with permission.

That discovery led me to think more deeply about the alligator's place in American history. Here was an animal that not only figured prominently in my childhood but also sat at the intersection of many of my scholarly interests: the history of natural history and wildlife conservation, environmental history, animal history, and American culture.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

MVB: Although Gator! is grounded in extensive historical research, I wrote it for a broad audience. I hope it will appeal not only to scholars and students of environmental, cultural, and animal history, but also to anyone interested in wildlife, Florida, and the myriad ways humans have interacted with the natural world. My goal was to tell a compelling story that would engage general readers while offering new insights for specialists.

I also hope readers will come away from the book with a sense of optimism. The American alligator's recovery is one of the great endangered species success stories. At a moment when environmental narratives often emphasize decline and loss, its story demonstrates that determined individuals and effective public policy can reverse even seemingly dire trends.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

MVB: One of the book's central themes is the complex, changing relationship between humans and wildlife. Over the past two centuries, Americans have feared alligators, hunted them, transformed them into cultural symbols, and ultimately worked to protect them. The alligator's story reveals how dramatically attitudes toward nature can change and how those changes can have profound consequences for the creatures with whom we share the landscape.

More broadly, Gator! is about the ways people create meaning around animals. The alligator has served as a feared predator, a revered totem, a commercial resource, a tourist attraction, an unlikely pet, an environmental indicator, and a symbol of Florida itself. By tracing these multiple meanings and how they have shifted through time, the book uses one remarkable reptile to tell a larger story about American culture, environmental change, and the complex connections between people and the natural world.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MVB: Much of the existing scholarship on North American apex predators has focused on wolves, coyotes, bears, and cougars. These studies have shown how deep-seated fear, folklore, concerns about livestock, and worries about safety fueled long-running campaigns to eliminate large mammalian predators from the landscape, pushing some to the brink of extinction.

The American alligator presents a strikingly different story. Although it has long inspired fear and anxiety, it largely escaped the systematic eradication campaigns that decimated many other North American predators. Instead, alligators came to occupy a distinctive place in American culture, particularly in Florida, where they were celebrated as symbols of the state's landscape, identity, and tourist economy even as they were hunted for their hides.

Gator! argues that the alligator's success is a result of changes in human attitudes and institutions. Although Floridians have long feared alligators, they have also celebrated them as symbols of the state's unique environment and identity. That combination of respect, pride, and concern helped foster legal protections and wildlife-management programs designed to reduce conflicts between people and alligators, including nuisance-alligator removal programs. The fact that an estimated 1.3 million alligators are thriving in a state with more than 23 million residents offers a hopeful example of coexistence between people and apex predators in an increasingly crowded world.

MB: What do you hope readers will take away from the book's story of the alligator?

MVB: I hope readers come away with a deeper appreciation for the American alligator and its place in our shared history. The alligator is neither a mindless killing machine nor a cuddly mascot. It is a powerful predator, an important part of the ecosystems it inhabits, and an animal that has left a surprisingly large imprint on the history and culture of both Florida and the United States more broadly.

I also hope readers gain a new appreciation for the ways animals shape human societies and the meanings we attach to them. The story of the alligator reminds us that our relationships with wildlife are never static. They evolve over time, shaped by changing cultural values, economic interests, and ideas about nature. Understanding those relationships can tell us a great deal about both the animals around us and ourselves.

item.title: Why You Should Try Group Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Why You Should Try Group Therapy

Group therapy is a uniquely powerful option that deserves to be more popular.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Group therapy promotes recovery through experiences of connection in a therapeutic community.
  • In group you observe yourself and others, notice unhelpful patterns, and practice new ones.
  • A variety of therapeutic groups can help reduce isolation, decrease shame and stigma, and cultivate hope.
  • More mental health professionals should consider training in and providing group therapies.

You should go to group therapy. I currently generally make a living by providing individual therapy and l still urge most people to consider giving some form of group therapy a shot.

Why Try Group Therapy?

  • Relationships are necessary for recovery. Isolation is a major contributor to hopelessness and connection is the way out of isolation. Connection facilitates hope and the struggle to cultivate hope is essential to recovery.
  • In your everyday life, you interact with non-clinicians on a far more regular basis than you meet with any kind of professional. Group therapy directly incorporates the interactions between group members to promote a process of positive change, which means everyone gains real experience using non-professional interactions for mutual growth.
  • A great deal of folks who pursue some form of therapy discover (or have validated) that in addition to things like depression and anxiety, there are also interpersonal problems which originate and/or exacerbate symptoms of mental health conditions. The treatment for such problems requires meaningful interpersonal practice.
  • Process group therapies that focus on relationships have inherent potential gains in helping with emotional regulation (Flores & Porges, 2017), a common interest for people seeking therapy.
  • In addition to everyday supportive interactions (which are also essential for recovery and personal growth), group psychotherapy is a distinct form of interaction where the group’s purpose, framework, and leaders are meant to facilitate connection that is uniquely and intentionally productive for treatment, meaning it includes active interventions that facilitate greater vulnerability and risk-taking, emotional richness, and interpersonal feedback.

A Very Brief History of Therapeutic Community

Dating back as early as the 1940s, the field of psychiatry began to treat relationships and community as an essential part of what makes treatment work, and leading hospitals then created and revised their programs with this as a central principle. In technical terms, Skinner (1979) defined the therapeutic milieu as “a scientific structuring of the environment in order to effect behavioral changes and to improve the psychological health and functioning of the individual.” In plain language, milieu therapy is based on the idea that people recover best in a therapeutic community, rather than merely in one-on-one relationships with providers. Although these two-person relationships are meaningful, there is unique power in multi-person relational experiences. Group psychotherapies provide an opportunity to be a part of a therapeutic community outside of a formal treatment programs or hospital.

Process Groups Are Powerhouses of Connection and Growth

Rooted in psychodynamic psychotherapy and different from educational, skills-based, or support groups, process groups are less structured and focus on the here-and-now relationships between group members. As members attend group, get to know each other, and interact as people, they can use the group as a relational playground to observe themselves and others, reflect upon how they form relationships, what works, what doesn’t, etc., and provide real-time feedback to one another (which is quite unusual in most everyday relationships!). This emphasis on unstructured, but contained (a lá Bion, 1961), relational risk-taking and mutual learning is a good dose of therapeutic community within everyday life—it is set apart from other aspects of daily life, but not disconnected from it. The intentional reprieve is safe, but temporary, and seeks to promote richer engagement with life outside of that space.

Typical Process Group Objectives

  1. Learn to use relationships (with people other than providers) to promote recovery.
    1. Increase connection and ability to meet one’s needs through developing interpersonal flexibility, “the ability to meet the demands of different situations such that one’s needs are met” (Whittingham, 2024).
  2. Use here-and-now interactions with group members to learn about patterns and problems of interest in your life.

Other Kinds of Groups

While this post emphasizes process groups, there are other ways to incorporate some form of group interaction and community into your journey towards relief and positive change, all of which can help reduce isolation, decrease shame and stigma, and cultivate hope.

  1. Psychotherapy/Process groups
    1. Facilitator is a professional mental health provider.
    2. Focus on group dynamics and therapeutic process for the group-as-a-whole as well as individual participants.
    3. Established treatment intervention within which there are specific evidence-based group modalities that are shown to promote recovery in treatment.
  2. Support groups
    1. Do not require a professional mental health provider. Typically FREE. Examples include:
      1. National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) chapters in practically every county across the United States.
      2. Refuge Recovery, AA, NA
      3. Postpartum Support International (PSI): support groups for a variety of fertility, pregnancy, birth, loss, and postpartum experiences.
    2. Participants support each other and give feedback or suggestions when asked.
    3. Support groups are beneficial to treatment and are often recommended as a supplement to other forms of treatment with a professional.
  3. Psychoeducational and/or Skills groups
    1. Facilitator is a professional healthcare or mental health provider.
    2. Focus is on education to increase understanding of oneself and mental health-related experiences and/or on teaching and practicing specific skills for coping or functioning, such as improving effective communication in relationships.
    3. These groups may be a part or form of evidence-based treatment such as a dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) or cognitive processing therapy (CPT) group or informed by clinical research and practice and led by an experienced professional in a specialty subject/issue.

Professional Call to Action

Successful encouragement for more people to try out group psychotherapy and other therapeutic group experiences depends on providers actually providing these services.

So to the professional audience, therapists, psychologists, psychiatrists, counsellors, etc., I encourage you to also consider expanding your clinical horizons and explore education and training on group psychotherapy and be a part of building more opportunities for therapeutic community and connection.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why So Many Women Watch Their Own Bodies From the Outside
item.description:
Body Image

Why So Many Women Watch Their Own Bodies From the Outside

A culture of objectification teaches women to see themselves as something to be looked at.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Women often learn to see and judge their bodies through other people's eyes.
  • Self-objectification can contribute to body dissatisfaction and disordered eating.
  • Shifting attention from how our bodies look to how they feel can help challenge self-objectification.
Source: Photo by Igor Rodrigues on Unsplash

The allegations in the Cornell 7 case have come up in my therapy sessions again and again over the past few weeks. While the specifics of the discourse varies from client to client, what I consistently hear in their reactions is recognition. Women know what it feels like to have their bodies treated as objects to be looked at and used. That experience is much older than the events at one fraternity house, and it shapes how many women relate to their own bodies every day.

Women have been pushing back against having their bodies judged for generations. In 1968, feminists protesting the Miss America pageant crowned a live sheep to make a point about women being judged like livestock. Nearly 60 years later, women are still being evaluated, and criticized, based on their appearance.

The standards may have changed somewhat, but the expectation that women's bodies are open to public scrutiny and judgment remains intact.

Learning to watch yourself

In 1997, psychologists Barbara Fredrickson and Tomi-Ann Roberts gave this a name: Objectification theory proposed that girls who grow up being watched and commented on can eventually take that outside view in and start monitoring their own bodies the way an observer would. They called this phenomenon self-objectification. People of every gender experience objectification, including men and nonbinary people. I'm focusing on women here because of the long history of judging women by their appearance, and because much of the research has focused on them.

A year later, Fredrickson and her colleagues published a study I still think about. College students tried on either a swimsuit or a sweater, alone in a dressing room, and then took a math test. The women in swimsuits did worse than the women in sweaters. The men's scores didn't change. Nobody was even watching them. Simply putting on a swimsuit seemed to shift the women's attention from the work in front of them to their appearance.

What's striking about that study is how little it took to distract the women from what they were doing. Nobody had to comment on their bodies or criticize how they looked. Just putting on a swimsuit was enough to distract them.

I think about how often this happens in everyday life. A woman sits through a meeting worrying about how her stomach looks in her chair. A teenager at the beach is so preoccupied with how she looks that she barely enjoys being there and avoids the water. It's hard to pay attention to what's happening around you when so much of your attention is focused on how you look. And there are psychological consequences: Research has found associations between self-objectification, body shame, and body dissatisfaction. Other studies have linked self-objectification to disordered eating.

What I see in my office

Many of my clients can tell me exactly how their body looks from across a room. They know which angles they avoid in photos and which clothes cover which parts. When I ask whether they're hungry or tired, they often go quiet for a long time. After years of watching the body from the outside, the inside has gotten hard to hear.

For people struggling with eating disorders, this disconnection can be especially difficult. Many of my clients have spent years following food rules, ignoring hunger, or judging their bodies based on appearance rather than how they feel. Over time, recognizing hunger, fullness, and other physical sensations can become increasingly difficult. Diet culture reinforces these patterns by praising restriction and treating control over eating as an accomplishment. Some of the very behaviors we worry about clinically are celebrated in everyday life.

Weight stigma only adds to the problem. Clients in larger bodies often tell me they feel stared at in the grocery store or at the doctor's office. It's as if their body is up for public discussion. That's objectification, too, even when it comes disguised as concern for health. And we know from research on weight stigma that these experiences are associated with greater risk for disordered eating.

Source: hoto by Dylann Hendricks | 딜란 on Unsplash

In my work with clients who struggle with eating disorders and body image, we spend a lot of time talking about what it means to experience your body rather than constantly evaluate it. Many clients are so accustomed to checking how they look that they barely realize they're doing it. They might catch their reflection in a store window, replay how they looked during a conversation, or spend an entire evening worrying about whether someone noticed their stomach wasn't flat or their lack of muscle tone. I ask clients to notice when this happens and what they feel in those moments. What were they doing before their attention shifted to their appearance? What did they stop noticing? We also work on paying more attention to physical sensations including hunger, fullness, comfort, and discomfort, which can be hard to recognize after years of focusing primarily on appearance.

We also talk about what reinforces these habits. For some clients, it's social media. For others, it's the constant conversation among friends or family about bodies, food, and weight. These ways of thinking develop over time, and changing them takes practice.

Whose eyes are we looking through?

When I ask clients what they think about their bodies, so often what they tell me is what they imagine other people think. They have become so accustomed to seeing themselves through someone else’s eyes that it’s difficult to separate their own feelings from the judgments they’ve learned to anticipate.

That’s what concerns me most about self-objectification. Even when nobody is looking, women can spend years living as though someone is. And while the allegations at Cornell may be an extreme example of women being treated as objects, the habit of looking at ourselves through other people’s eyes is far more ordinary. It’s worth asking how much of our relationship with our bodies actually belongs to us.

item.title: Transmuting Intergenerational Trauma With Art
item.description:
Trauma

Transmuting Intergenerational Trauma With Art

The healing power of art.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Tuan Andrew Nguyen has created a work of public art that is designed to help heal intergenerational trauma.
  • This follows in the tradition of great public art, including the work of Rodin and Maya Lin.
  • The work was inspired by the destruction of the ancient statues in Bamiyan, Afghanistan, by the Taliban.

In the heart of New York City, a 27-foot-tall Buddha stands in the company of steel and glass skyscrapers. Located on the High Line, an elevated oasis of flowers and greenery on the city’s West Side, it speaks eloquently to the transmutation of intergenerational trauma. As a clinical psychologist who has treated trauma for more than 30 years, an art historian, and a meditation teacher, this transformative and integrative creation of public art has captured my attention and imagination.

A Tribute to the Destroyed Buddhas of Bamiyan

Called "The Light that Shines Through the Universe," the sculpture is the brainchild of Vietnamese American artist Tuan Andrew Nguyen. It is a tribute to the memory of the Buddhas of Bamiyan, a celebrated archeological site in Afghanistan. The Buddhas were carved into the massive cliff in the Bamiyan Valley 1,500 years ago. The valley was part of the Silk Road trade route, an intersection between China, India, and Persia that fostered cultural, economic, and religious exchange. The statues were dramatically destroyed by the Taliban in 2001, leaving empty caverns where the Buddhas used to be.

In an interview with Tricycle Magazine (Fall 2026), Nguyen speaks about his vision and intention for this work of public art. “The Buddhas of Bamiyan have always carried for me a profound lesson about the impermanence and instability of what we imagine to be permanent.”

A Cognitive Reframe

He witnessed the destruction on television when he was in his mid-20s. As he processed the event, he took a wide view; he didn’t focus only on the destruction or the loss of a heritage site. He took a more profound perspective, or what we call a “cognitive reframe.” He reflected on the idea of Buddhist idea of emptiness. “In Buddhist philosophy, emptiness is not simply about absence or loss—it’s a space for potential.”

What is remarkable about this unique work of public art (which follows in the tradition of Rodin’s "The Thinker" and Maya Lin’s Vietnam Veterans Memorial) is the focus on the potential for healing. The NYC Buddha has two parts—a sandstone body (carved by master stone sculptors) and brass hands, held by metal poles, which evoke prosthetic limbs. The metal for the hands came from artillery shells found in Afghanistan and Vietnam. They glow with light when the sun touches them. They are in the classic mudras (or postures) of fearlessness (Abhaya) and giving blessings and compassion (Varada). What is profound is that the artist takes the materials of war and destruction and turns them into objects of peace and resilience.

The Possibility of Healing

When we look at the sculpture, we are moved by the monumental presence, the heartbreak of loss, and the ubiquity of violence, but above all, the possibility of healing. The Buddha, in its component parts, holds the possibility that we have the imagination, energy, and courage to create a better future for all.

I practice meditation at Cambridge Insight Meditation Center, where I’ve been studying with a remarkable teacher, Narayan Helen Liebenson, for decades. Last week, at the end of a “daily dharma” drop-in class where hundreds of people gather for a free Zoom 15-minute meditation class, Narayan suggested that we all send prayers and blessings to the entire world. I was inspired by hundreds of us sending blessings to the entire world. I feel that this corresponds to what Nguyen is doing in his sculpture—sending compassion, peace, and reconciliation to the world with his work of art.

I had not yet seen the High Line Buddha, but I was holding the meditation practice in mind when I was in the presence of this remarkable and visionary work of art. This was the prayer I offered, based on a traditional loving-kindness meditation:

“May all beings be Safe and Healthy. May all beings be free of suffering and ill-will. May we all be Peaceful and live in Wisdom and Compassion. May we treat each other with kindness and respect.”

Can we, guided by our artists and spiritual teachers, send blessings out to this suffering world?

item.title: The Lucky Bastard Club
item.description:
Guilt

The Lucky Bastard Club

Survivor guilt and cognitive immobility.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Guilt involves perceived responsibility and can also come from surviving traumatic event that others did not.
  • Veterans may feel shame and anxiety when discussing their wartime experiences.
  • Cognitive immobility can help us explain why some veterans remain mentally attached to war zones.

The most troubling part of all this is that I actually liked being in Afghanistan. I didn’t want to leave. For the first year or so after we got back, I spoke openly and bluntly about the experience. Eventually, however, I started to notice a pattern: Whenever I talked about it, I’d leave the conversation feeling ashamed and become increasingly anxious over the rest of the day. So, I decided to stop bringing it up.

These words appeared in a New York Times report written by Sgt Adam Linehan, a former US Army combat medic who served in Afghanistan from 2010 to 2011. His admission that he missed being in a war zone is common among veterans. Former US Army Major and chaplain Carlos C. Huerta has expressed similar feelings.

At the time, Linehan was experiencing sleepless nights, seeking solace in alcohol and drugs, and suffering panic attacks. One night, his wife, Sara, found him ‘... doubled over at the foot of the bed’ following a panic attack. He told her, ‘Joining the Army was a mistake’.

Linehan described his longing for Afghanistan as ‘troubling’. However, his desire to return to the war zone suggests he missed something about life there and struggled to adjust to civilian life after returning to the US. His experience reflects a familiar feeling among some veterans: ‘They came home but could not find the home they left behind…’.

The guilt of being a ‘lucky bastard’

For some who survive war, being alive can bring a painful burden known as survivor guilt.

According to a recent study, content survivor guilt occurs when someone feels responsible for another person’s death because of something they did or failed to do. Existential survivor guilt arises when someone feels guilty simply for being alive when others have died, even though they know they were not responsible for those deaths.

Sgt Linehan’s grandfather, Michael Linehan Jr., a former US B-24 pilot, survived World War II and joined the Lucky Bastard Club, a club for a group of airmen who survived the war. However, surviving war did not necessarily mean escaping guilt. Sgt Linehan never wanted to join that club, but he, too, came to experience the burden of survivor guilt.

For some veterans, guilt and shame can follow them for much of their lives, made worse by a painful sense of unfairness about who survives and who does not.

You can be a clerk typist and get hit by a rocket while at a Vietnamese massage parlour in Saigon. You can be an infantryman and not get a scratch in 12 months.

To survive, then, is to be a lucky bastard.

The guilt that follows them home

Sgt Linehan struggled with the guilt of surviving war. For Staff Sergeant Robert Miltenberger, however, it was something he said during a firefight in Iraq that continued to haunt him. He had lied to a wounded soldier, Tomas Young, in an attempt to reassure him. The lie still haunts him, and Miltenberger recounted the story with a quaking voice:

I had one soldier, he kept saying, ‘I’m paralysed, I’m paralysed’. I said, ‘No you’re not, everybody’s just laying on you’. There was nobody laying on him.

Young was just 24 and had been in Iraq for less than two weeks when a sniper’s bullet damaged his spinal cord, leaving him paralysed from the chest down. Miltenberger carried the guilt for years and had not seen Young since. Nearly 10 years later, with the help of ABC News, Miltenberger travelled with his wife from Cameron, Louisiana, to Portland, Oregon, to reunite with Young and ‘try and find some peace for that survivor's guilt all these years later’.

When they met, Young, whose speech was slurred, spoke first:

‘I bared no grudge against you’, Young tells Miltenberger.

‘Well, I lied to you’, Miltenberger answers.

‘You were just trying to help me’, Young says.

‘I was feeling guilty because I didn’t get shot’, Miltenberger says.

The consequences of war weighed heavily on them and they struggled to the point of contemplating taking their own lives. Guilt and painful memories followed them long after the fighting ended.

Final thoughts

Survivor guilt can be common among veterans, but Sgt Linehan suggested that something else may lie beneath it. He told PBS NewsHour:

So, if you would ask me if I felt guilty for anything I did in Afghanistan around the time that I started to kind of have this breakdown, I would have said no. The guilt is masking something else, because when I was over there, and I saw these things, I felt afraid, and – but I didn't feel sad. And so, I thought, I don't have a right to say I have PTSD, because, when I saw it happen, I didn't feel anything.

Linehan’s account raises a broader question about the psychological struggles veterans face that may not fit neatly into diagnoses such as PTSD. This concern is shared by Dr Hannah Murray of the University of Oxford, who has said:

I believe some people have emotional consequences from trauma that aren’t PTSD, and because of the way the health care systems work here and in America, they won’t get taken care of’ … So, I think there are a lot of people coming home from war who don’t get treatment and end up making bad decisions.

These accounts highlight the need to better understand veterans’ psychological struggles to provide appropriate support. When Linehan said, 'I actually liked being in Afghanistan’, his words may have reflected more than a cry for help. His experience may relate to ‘mental immobilisation to the past’, a psychological attachment to earlier experiences that may contribute to ‘a disrupted sense of identity and home’, two key features of cognitive immobility.

His remarks alone cannot establish that he experienced cognitive immobility, but they raise questions about why some veterans may long for life in a war zone long after they have returned and why so many struggle to adjust to civilian life after their military service has ended.

For veterans and those supporting them, recognising that leaving a war zone does not always mean leaving it behind psychologically may help explain the difficulties they have adjusting to civilian life and finding a sense of belonging at home.

item.title: How Nature and Nurture Contribute to Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Intergenerational Trauma

How Nature and Nurture Contribute to Intergenerational Trauma

Transgenerational epigenetics fuse with learned behavior to perpetuate the trauma cycle.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • Perpetuation of intergenerational trauma requires learned behavior and activation of genetic proclivities.
  • Intergenerational trauma can take the form of borderline personality disorder.
  • Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance likely plays a large role in borderline personality disorder.
Source: Mirerek8 / Pixabay

A friend of mine recently asked, “Do you believe in intergenerational trauma?” My affirmative answer
spurred his curiosity: “But how does someone’s, say, war trauma that happened to them get passed to another generation?” More wondering emanated from the passenger seat about next generations getting vicarious trauma from hearing war stories. Then something about perhaps genes can be altered by trauma to encourage hypervigilance and aggressive reactivity in offspring as a preemptive strike against potential trauma of their own.

Both of my compadre’s ideas are viable possibilities, vicarious trauma being a well-researched topic, and trauma-induced genetic alteration is an emerging area of research interest. Evidence does exist (e.g., Chou et al., 2024) that environmental stimuli “can be written into heritable material…and persist to the next generation,” which primes the new generation for how to respond to traumatically stressful environmental stimuli, sort of like my friend hypothesized.

In any event, it is not that someone’s specific traumatic experience gets passed down, like each succeeding generation has flashbacks of their great-great-grandfather’s World War I incidents. Rather, like most things in psychology, there is a complex interplay of nature and nurture lending itself to generational perpetuation of the pervasive chaos of one person’s long-ago trauma.

Borderline personality disorder as intergenerational trauma

My favorite illustration of this is borderline personality disorder (BPD). The foundation of BPD tends to be abandonment/rejection by an early attachment figure(s). As the person ages, their lives revolve around fear of abandonment/rejection. Numerous maladaptive behaviors/defenses follow, like reactive rage, self-destructive activities, identity disturbances (such as chameleonizing to various people/groups, for who would want to reject one of their own?), attention-seeking, and a push-pull attachment style.

Further, people with BPD have genetic/brain anomalies (e.g., Ansari et al., 2023) including amygdalar hypersensitivity, low serotonin, and an underperforming prefrontal cortex that contribute to activating anxiety, poor impulse control, anger, and aggression. Researchers (e.g., Plunk & Richards, 2020) have shown that how genes are expressed, or turned on and off, can be influenced by environmental factors in a process called DNA methylation. This can influence gene expression in next generations, known as transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. BPD researchers (e.g., Dawidowski et al., 2025) are finding increasing evidence that this plays a large role in the development of BPD.

An illustrative case

The story of Eddie and Jeanine, and their following generations, illustrates how this comes together for intergenerational trauma. It is based on a real example, and all names and some details have been changed:
Three generations ago, Eddie doted over Jeanine. They married quickly, bought a house, and had two kids, making for increased bills. Thus, Eddie worked more and would spend time doting over the kids when home and less over Jeanine, but still was a good husband. Jeanine began wondering if Eddie was working more shifts to avoid her. After all, he seemed more interested in the kids, and their romance declined.

Never financially responsible, Jeanine suggested they open another credit card to cut back on Eddie’s work schedule; Eddie explained credit cards need to be paid off in a timely fashion, so it wouldn’t make a difference. “Clearly, this is an excuse,” thought Jeanine. She became cold toward Eddie, even aggressive if he came home later than usual. “Is he having an affair?” she thought. She wasn’t going to be ignored. Jeanine began getting together more frequently with high-school friends and gave her version of the story. One friend, Jeff, saw her as a damsel in distress, and one thing led to another.

Jeanine idealized him as her “savior” from a lousy, “cheating” husband and left her family to live with him. The kids, ages 2 and 3 at the time, saw her periodically and were confused about why she left home, rendering the rise of their own feelings of abandonment. Eddie had the kids most of the time, but with shared custody, they sometimes stayed with Jeanine. There, they witnessed domestic violence and Jeanine kicking Jeff out of his own house if he didn’t meet her expectations, an echo of her family-of-origin dynamics.

Little Penelope always identified with Jeanine in her malleable years, given she was the female attachment figure. At Jeff’s house, she didn’t like a lot of what she saw, but Penelope somehow felt this was how one was supposed to relate to others. With age, her own fears of abandonment heightened; if one’s mother would simply take off, anyone could. She was always looking for evidence that someone was about to reject her. She’d push people away in a preemptive strike if she suspected pending rejection, a common BPD defense (i.e., “I pushed them away; they didn’t reject me!”). Eventually she would realize her error and pull them back in, but also let them know how disappointed she was for “making” her feel rejected.

Source: Andrea Piacquadio / Pixabay

As Penelope began dating, the dynamic matured. She would even be physically aggressive with some guys, raging at them if she saw them socializing with another girl. Other times she would self-destruct, cutting herself in punishment for feeling she must not be good enough if, as she perceived it, a boyfriend needed any girl’s attention but hers.

Penelope’s early attachment trauma began taking its toll. She demanded attention and guarantees of nonrejection. She would sexually saturate any guy she dated, because what guy would want to get rid of that? Her only demand was that they spend every second together. The guys quickly felt emotionally suffocated; the relationships became tumultuous and would abruptly end. She became pregnant and married the child’s father. Soon, little Bobby was immersed in watching one or the other parent leave for periods and not see them. Later, Penelope was sometimes passed out drunk in the mornings, and thus, Bobby was often absent from school. This led to DCF investigations and a series of removals over the years.

Not surprisingly, Bobby found it difficult to relate to others due to the attachment trauma, influencing his gene expression and evolution of BPD, and the cycle continued.

Generations of inherited proclivities coupled with exposure to traumatic events that shape interpersonal behaviors and activate genetic traits create a perfect storm that, in some cases, eternally perpetuates the intergenerational trauma.

The information should not replace personalized care or intervention from an individual’s provider or formal supervision if you’re a practitioner or student.

item.title: Why the Idea of a Loneliness Epidemic Won't Die
item.description:
Loneliness

Why the Idea of a Loneliness Epidemic Won't Die

Calling loneliness an epidemic gets attention but sends money to the wrong fixes.

Posted October 27, 2026

Key points
  • An epidemic is a sudden rise above expected levels. Loneliness trends show stability or slow drift.
  • The epidemic label points to social media and away from income, safety nets, and public space.
  • When hyped findings shrink, practitioners stop trusting research, as education has shown.

I have asked several colleagues why they keep calling loneliness an epidemic. More than one gave me the same answer. They know the word is not quite right, but it gets the topic into newspapers and onto ministers' desks. I understand the temptation, because the word works. In 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General titled his advisory Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation. But a word also tells people where to look for a fix, and this one points the wrong way.

What an Epidemic Is

In public health, an epidemic is an increase in cases above what is normally expected in a population, often a sudden one. The word suggests something new with an agent you can find and remove, the way cholera led John Snow to the Broad Street pump in 1854. Loneliness has been measured for decades, so the question is whether it has risen suddenly.

What the Trends Show

For older adults, mostly not. Among Americans over 50, the share reporting loneliness fell from 20.1% to 15.5% between 1996 and 2018. Younger groups show more change. Loneliness in emerging adults rose slowly from 1976 to 2019 and stayed flat after 2012. Midlife loneliness crept up across generations in the United States and parts of Europe, while it held steady or fell in Nordic and continental Europe. A slow drift in some places and stability in others is not an epidemic.

What Our Reanalysis of Isolation Found

Loneliness is a feeling. Social isolation is an objective state, often measured as time spent alone, and plenty of people who spend time alone do not feel lonely. The advisory treated the two together and also cited a 2023 study of the American Time Use Survey that reported rising time alone from 2003 to 2020, with a sharp acceleration after 2018. When the authors declined to share their code, we organized six independent teams to reproduce the analysis, which I summarized here last year. Leaving out the pandemic year halved the apparent rise. What remained was about 24 more minutes alone per day over 17 years, a small effect (Cohen's d = 0.10). In follow-up work that is not yet published, Federico D'Atri and Randy McCarthy traced much of even this rise to who was surveyed. Over the years the data included more older adults, who spend more time alone. Differences between groups were far larger. Adults over 65 spent 231 more minutes a day alone than adults aged 25 to 34, nearly ten times the change over time. People without paid work spent 144 more minutes alone than those working 50 hours or more, and people with household incomes under $25,000 spent 98 more minutes alone than those earning over $100,000.

What the Label Does to Solutions

An epidemic calls for a new agent, and for loneliness the usual suspect is the smartphone. In three datasets covering more than 350,000 adolescents, digital technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being. A cause that small cannot carry the epidemic story.

The larger factors are older. Middle-aged adults in Denmark, the Netherlands, and Sweden report the lowest loneliness of 14 countries studied, and the authors point to strong safety nets. Low income raises loneliness in later life, less so where welfare spending is generous. In our interviews in Türkiye, people kept coming back to money. Income, working hours, housing, and public space have no villain and no quick fix, so they make poor headlines. My colleague Neil Lewis Jr pointed me to Winners Take All (2018) by Anand Giridharadas, who described a similar pull, where funders favor solutions that leave the systems behind a problem intact. When the epidemic frame points at screens, budgets follow, and the larger levers go unused.

A Warning From Education

When we discussed these kinds of topics, Neil and another colleague, Andrew Przybylski, pointed me to education that has lived through this cycle. Controlled tests never supported learning styles, yet belief in them among educators remains high. Growth mindset was sold as a game changer, and a large meta-analysis found small average effects on achievement. Teachers in training who read research contradicting their beliefs tended to doubt the research itself, and learning-styles researchers warn that hype undermines trust in education research as a whole. Loneliness research is on the same road. If we promise an epidemic and a fix that turns out weak, city officials, employers, and clinicians will discount the next findings, including the ones that hold up.

Saying How Ready the Evidence Is

In 2020, colleagues and I proposed evidence readiness levels, modeled on NASA's technology readiness levels. The scale runs from early findings that need refining, through tests in real settings, to evidence ready for large-scale rollout. Most findings in our field had not reached the top.

The link between social connection and health rests on decades of long-term data. Claims that an app, a workplace program, or a screen-time limit will reduce loneliness at scale usually rest on far less. Naming the level lets a mayor or an HR leader judge how much weight a claim can bear.

There is a frame that wins attention without overstating the trend: Brain capital treats people's brain health and skills as an economic asset, and social connection is one of its drivers. An asset invites questions about investment and return, and those questions lead back to income, working hours, and public space.

Colleagues who use the epidemic label for attention could use the same platform to report the rate, the trend, and who is most affected, and say how ready the evidence for each fix is. If you fund programs, ask for that before you sign.
